title: Fearless, changeless
hook: the Jaap keeps returning to fearlessness, a quality at the heart of the Khalsa ideal

segments.voice: Yesterday, ek achhari, the one-letter meter, and your line, ajai, alai, abhai, abai. Today, the third of those four words, the one Jaap keeps coming back to.

Fear has a body. A tight chest before the phone call. Cold hands before the exam results open. A stomach that drops when the boss says, got a minute? Plenty of people carry a few fears around like stones in a pocket: money, health, being left, being found out. The weight gets so familiar they forget it's there, until something makes them reach in and touch one. Jaap Sahib, recited every morning, keeps saying one word against that weight.
screen: `FEAR HAS A BODY.` → `STONES IN A POCKET.` → `A WORD SAID AGAINST THE WEIGHT.`

segments.voice: The word is abhai. Bhai is fear; a is without. Fearless. It's in the one-letter meter, and it returns again and again in other stanzas beside its partners: unconquerable, unchanging, unborn. Of all the qualities Jaap praises, fearlessness is one it simply won't let go of. Sikhs met the idea long before Jaap. The Mool Mantar, at the very start of the Guru Granth Sahib, calls the One nirbhau, without fear, and nirvair, without hatred, side by side. Guru Nanak's opening and the Tenth Guru's praise agree. Then comes the turn that matters for daily life: Sikhs don't praise fearlessness only as something God has. They hope to grow toward it. The ninth Guru, Guru Tegh Bahadur, the Tenth Guru's father, wrote that the wise person is the one who frightens no one, and fears no one. Both halves: not a bully, and not a coward. Sikhs remember him living it; tradition tells of him going to Delhi and to his execution rather than abandon the freedom of others to practice their faith. Fearlessness sits at the heart of the Khalsa ideal his son founded: a people meant to stand up without fear and without hate, and never to put fear into the innocent. As Sikh teachers often put it, people grow a little like what they praise every morning. Saying abhai doesn't make fear vanish. The hope is that fear stops being the one deciding.
screen: `ABHAI: WITHOUT FEAR.` · `NIRBHAU, NIRVAIR: THE MOOL MANTAR.` · `FRIGHTEN NO ONE, FEAR NO ONE.` · `GROWING LIKE WHAT YOU PRAISE.` · then, large: `FEARLESS LIKE HIM.`

segments.voice: Pick up one stone from the pocket and name it, silently and plainly: I'm afraid of this. Notice where it sits in your body, chest, stomach, shoulders, jaw, and breathe into that place without trying to make the fear leave. If you like, say abhai on the out-breath a few times, not to argue with the fear, just to remind it who else is here.
Abhai. Without fear: the quality Jaap keeps returning to, echoing nirbhau in the Mool Mantar.
Your line: fearless like him. Frighten no one, and fear no one. Day three hundred fifty-two, done.

howItsDone: Sikhs say nirbhau, without fear, every day in the Mool Mantar and abhai many times in Jaap Sahib, and fearlessness without hatred is central to the Khalsa ideal.

options: fears no one, and frightens no one.
fears nothing, and cares about nothing.

original.note: Gurmukhi: abhai, without fear, from bhai, fear; compare nirbhau in the Mool Mantar.

trapdoor: what you thought: fearless is a quality only God has.
what it means: Sikhs praise the One as fearless and hope to grow toward it, frightening no one and fearing no one.
what a scholar hears: abhai in Jaap parallels nirbhau in the Mool Mantar; Guru Tegh Bahadur's salok at Ang 1427 sets out the human ideal.
recall: sound, often the deep sound of the Divine
a devotee, someone devoted to God

chat.says: Is fearlessness just something God has, or something Sikhs try for too?
options: Both: Jaap calls the One abhai, and Sikhs hope to grow toward it: fear no one, frighten no one.
Only God; people can't really change, so praising fearlessness won't touch our fears.
Sikhs try for it, and fearless means being able to frighten anyone who threatens you.
chat.meaning: Jaap keeps returning to abhai, fearless; Guru Tegh Bahadur wrote that the wise one frightens no one and fears no one.
